nameStory: The Decorated Pholiota gets its fancy name from the striking brown scales that cover its cap and stem like ornate decorations on a fancy cake. These pointed, curved scales give the mushroom such a distinctive appearance that scientists eventually decided it deserved its own special genus, Leucopholiota, which means 'white Pholiota' referring to its bright white gills.
description: The Decorated Pholiota is a showy woodland mushroom that looks like it's wearing ornate armor made of brown scales. Its cap and stem are covered with distinctive pointed, curved brown scales that make it stand out against the forest floor. The contrast between these dark decorative scales and the bright white gills underneath creates a striking appearance that's hard to miss when you're exploring New England's hardwood forests.

idTips.label: Cap
idTips.description: Covered with distinctive pointed brown scales that curve outward like tiny shingles or armor plates, giving it a very decorative, almost artificial appearance

idTips.label: Gills
idTips.description: Bright white and closely spaced, creating a stark contrast with the brown scaly cap above

idTips.label: Stem
idTips.description: Also covered with the same pointed brown scales as the cap, continuing the decorative pattern down the entire mushroom

idTips.label: Substrate
idTips.description: Always grows on or near decaying hardwood logs and stumps, acting as nature's recycler

idTips.label: Texture
idTips.description: The scales feel dry and papery to the touch, not slimy or sticky like some other woodland mushrooms

habitat: Look for Decorated Pholiota in New England's mixed and hardwood forests, especially around decaying logs, stumps, and fallen branches of oak, maple, and other deciduous trees. It prefers shaded woodland areas with rich, moist soil where fallen wood can slowly decompose. You'll often find it in small groups rather than alone, typically in the same spots year after year.

seasonality.spring: Rarely seen in spring, though mycelium may be actively working through decaying wood underground preparing for later fruiting.
seasonality.summer: Begins to appear in mid to late summer after periods of warm, humid weather and adequate rainfall on decaying hardwood.
seasonality.fall: Peak season for finding these decorative mushrooms, especially after September rains when they fruit most abundantly on rotting logs.
seasonality.winter: Completely absent above ground, but the mycelium continues breaking down wood beneath the snow and forest litter.

funFact: This mushroom has been such a taxonomic wanderer that it's been placed in six different genera since 1873, like a fungal nomad that scientists couldn't figure out where to house until they finally gave up and created an entirely new genus just for it and its close relatives!
confusionNotes: Most likely confused with Pholiota squarrosoides, which also has scaly caps, but the Decorated Pholiota's scales are more pointed and curved, and its gills stay bright white rather than becoming yellowish. Remember: if the scales look like tiny curved daggers and the gills are pure white, you've found the decorated one.
contextualKnowledge: Despite its name containing 'Pholiota,' this mushroom was moved out of that genus entirely and now sits in its own genus Leucopholiota, showing how our understanding of fungal relationships continues to evolve with genetic research. The name change reflects its unique characteristics that set it apart from true Pholiota species.
compareHints: Since it's the only Leucopholiota species commonly found in New England, compare it to the related Pholiota species which have similar scaly appearances but less pronounced, pointed scales. The Decorated Pholiota's scales are more dramatically curved and pointed outward, while true Pholiota species tend to have flatter, less ornate scales and often develop yellowish rather than pure white gills.
